label: Digitally Immersed & Emotionally Strained
summary: This profile represents highly educated women who spend substantial time on social media (averaging nearly 4 hours daily, with many exceeding 5 hours) and report elevated levels of loneliness, depressive symptoms, and anxiety. Across all three psychological distress measures—loneliness (UCLA-8 mean ≈ 1.78), depression (PHQ-9 mean ≈ 1.81), and anxiety (GAD-7 mean ≈ 2.27)—scores are consistently above moderate thresholds, with anxiety being the most pronounced. This cluster of 140 respondents suggests a pattern in which heavy social-media engagement co-occurs with broad emotional distress.
demographic_anchor: Female, graduate-level education or above, daily social-media use exceeding 5 hours
behavior_markers: Heavy daily social-media consumption averaging approximately 3.9 hours, with a substantial portion exceeding 5 hours
Elevated loneliness scores indicating persistent feelings of social disconnection despite high digital engagement
Moderate-to-high depressive symptom levels suggesting recurring low mood and reduced motivation
Notably high anxiety symptoms, the most elevated distress indicator in this profile
Pattern of co-occurring psychological distress across multiple domains alongside intensive screen-based social activity
tone: Concerned and empathetic, reflecting the convergence of heavy digital engagement with significant emotional vulnerability

label: Well-Adjusted Light-Use Graduate Male
summary: This profile represents male respondents with graduate-level education who report lower loneliness, lower depressive symptoms, and lower anxiety compared to other profiles. They engage in relatively light daily social-media use, averaging roughly 2.8 hours per day (within the 1–3 hour bracket). Their psychological well-being indicators are consistently favorable, with notably low scores on loneliness (UCLA-8 mean ≈ 0.78), depression (PHQ-9 mean ≈ 0.27), and anxiety (GAD-7 mean ≈ 0.03).

Pattern of moderate, non-excessive digital engagement
tone: Stable, emotionally balanced, and psychologically resilient

label: Lonely but Low-Distress Heavy Scroller
summary: This profile captures highly educated women who spend nearly 5 hours per day on social media and report elevated loneliness, yet exhibit comparatively low levels of depressive and anxiety symptoms. Despite heavy digital engagement, their psychological distress remains below average on clinical screening measures, suggesting that their social-media use coexists with emotional resilience even as perceived social connection remains lacking.

label: Well-Adjusted Light-Use Graduate Male
summary: This profile represents a relatively large group (n = 217) of male respondents with graduate-level education who report low loneliness, minimal depressive symptoms, and low anxiety. Their daily social-media use is light, averaging roughly 1.6 hours per day (within the 1–3 hour range). Across all psychological well-being indicators, this group scores well below scale midpoints, suggesting generally positive mental health and moderate digital engagement.
